mainEntity.name: Why must a public class name match its filename in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: The Java compiler uses the public class name to generate the .class file. Since one .java file can contain only one public class, the filename must match that public class name exactly (including case) so the compiler knows where to look. If they don't match, javac throws: 'class X is public, should be declared in a file named X.java'.

Yes, Java is fully case-sensitive. System, system, and SYSTEM are three completely different identifiers. System.out.println() works because System is the exact class name. Writing system.out.println() gives a compile error. This applies to every identifier — class names, variable names, method names, and keywords.

mainEntity.name: What are the rules for naming identifiers in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Java identifiers must start with a letter (A–Z or a–z), underscore (_), or dollar sign ($). Subsequent characters can include digits (0–9), letters, _, or $. They cannot be Java reserved keywords, cannot contain spaces or special characters like @, #, !, and cannot start with a digit. Java supports Unicode characters in identifiers.

mainEntity.name: How many keywords does Java have?

acceptedAnswer.text: Java has 67 reserved keywords as of Java 21. These include standard keywords like class, int, for, while, if, else, return, and also reserved-but-unused keywords like const and goto. Java 21 also introduced contextual keywords like record, sealed, permits, yield, and when — which have special meaning only in specific contexts.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between a statement and an expression in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: An expression evaluates to a value — for example, a + b, Math.max(5, 10), or x > 0. A statement is a complete executable instruction that ends with a semicolon or a block — for example, int x = 5 + 3; or System.out.println(x);. An expression becomes a statement when you add a semicolon and it has a side effect, like x++;

articleHeader.title: Java Syntax — The Complete Guide
articleHeader.subtitle: Master the fundamental rules and structure of Java code — from class declarations and statements to identifiers, keywords, whitespace rules, and the anatomy of every Java program.

blocks.text: Java syntax is the set of rules that defines how Java programs are written and interpreted by the compiler. Just as English has grammar rules (subject, verb, object), Java has syntax rules that every valid Java program must follow — without exception.

Unlike Python which uses indentation to define code blocks, or JavaScript which is loosely typed, Java has strict, unambiguous syntax rules. The compiler (javac) rejects any program that violates these rules before execution ever happens. This strictness is a feature — it catches bugs at compile time, not at runtime in production.

Key insight: Java's strict syntax means 100% of type mismatches, missing semicolons, and structural errors are caught by the compiler — your code either compiles perfectly or tells you exactly what's wrong.

Every valid Java program must follow a precise structural hierarchy. Understanding this hierarchy is the single most important foundation for writing Java. The annotated code below shows every component of a real Java program:
The 5 structural layers of every Java program
Java code is built from three fundamental building blocks that you must understand before writing any program:
Statements
A statement is a complete unit of execution — like a sentence in English. Every statement in Java must end with a semicolon (;). Missing a semicolon is one of the most common beginner errors.

blocks.label: Statements.java
lines: // Control flow statement (no semicolon — has a block)

blocks.text: Expressions
An expression is any combination of values, variables, operators, and method calls that evaluates to a single value. Expressions form the core of statements.
Blocks
A block is a group of statements enclosed in curly braces { }. Blocks define scope — variables declared inside a block are only accessible within that block.

blocks.label: Blocks.java
lines: public class Blocks {               // class block — outermost
public static void main(String[] args) {  // method block
int bonus = 10;          // only visible inside this block
// System.out.println(bonus); → ERROR: bonus out of scope

blocks.text: Keywords are reserved words with special meaning in Java. They are part of the language specification and cannot be used as identifiers (variable names, method names, class names). Java has 67 reserved keywords as of Java 21.
Common trap: const and goto are reserved keywords in Java but are not currently used. You cannot use them as identifiers, even though they have no functional meaning.

Java 21 contextual keywords: var, record, sealed, permits, yield, and when are special — they have keyword meaning only in specific contexts and can be used as variable names (though you should avoid it for clarity).
An identifier is the name you give to any Java element — classes, methods, variables, packages, constants. Java has strict rules for what constitutes a valid identifier.
Legal identifier rules

items.text: Must start with a letter (A–Z, a–z), underscore (_), or dollar sign ($)
Subsequent characters can include digits (0–9), letters, _, or $
No length limit — but keep them readable
Unicode characters are supported (e.g., int मूल्य = 10; is valid)
Cannot be a Java keyword (class, int, for, etc.)
Cannot contain spaces, hyphens (-), or special chars like @, #, !

blocks.label: Identifiers.java
lines: // int my score;     → space not allowed

blocks.text: Comments are ignored completely by the Java compiler. They exist for human readers — explaining intent, documenting APIs, and annotating complex logic. Java supports three types of comments:

blocks.label: Comments.java
lines: // 1. Single-line comment — from // to end of line
* Useful for temporarily disabling code blocks
* 3. Javadoc comment — used by javadoc tool to generate HTML docs
* @return          time in hours as a double
public static double calculateTime(int distance, int speed) {

blocks.text: Professional practice: Every public class and public method in production Java code should have a Javadoc comment. This is how Java's own API documentation (docs.oracle.com) is generated — directly from source code comments.

Java is not whitespace-sensitive like Python. The compiler ignores extra spaces, tabs, and blank lines between tokens. However, at least one whitespace character is required to separate keywords and identifiers from each other.

blocks.label: Whitespace.java
lines: // All three are identical to the compiler:
// Version 2 — everything on one line (valid but unreadable)
public class Hello{public static void main(String[] args){System.out.println("Hello");}}
public   static   void   main( String[]   args )   {

blocks.text: Industry standard: Java projects use 4-space indentation per block level. The Google Java Style Guide and Oracle's Code Conventions both specify this. Your IDE will handle indentation automatically — Ctrl+Alt+L in IntelliJ, Ctrl+Shift+F in Eclipse.
Java is fully case-sensitive. Every letter's case matters — in class names, method names, variable names, and keywords. This is one of the most common sources of beginner errors.

blocks.label: CaseSensitivity.java
lines: // Keywords must be lowercase — these are invalid as keywords:
// Int, INT, For, WHILE → these become identifiers, not keywords
// int Int = 10;  ← valid! 'Int' is an identifier here, not a keyword

blocks.text: Naming rules define what is legal. Naming conventions define what is standard. These conventions are universally followed in Java codebases worldwide. Violating them won't cause a compile error, but it will make your code stand out as unprofessional.

public void depositAmount(double amount) {       // method: camelCase

lines: // Sealed class — restricts which classes can extend it
public sealed class Shape permits Circle, Rectangle, Triangle {}
public final class Circle    extends Shape { double radius; }
public final class Rectangle extends Shape { double width, height; }
public final class Triangle  extends Shape { double base, height; }
// The compiler now knows every possible Shape subtype — enables exhaustive pattern matching

blocks.text: These are the most commonly asked Java Syntax interview questions for freshers and beginner-level positions. Master these before any Java interview.

items.q: Q1. Why must a public class name match its filename in Java?
items.a: The Java compiler uses the public class name to generate the .class file. Since one .java file can contain only one public class, the filename must match that public class name exactly (including case) so the compiler knows where to look. If they don't match, javac throws: 'class X is public, should be declared in a file named X.java'.

items.q: Q2. Is Java case-sensitive? Give an example.
items.a: Yes, Java is fully case-sensitive. System, system, and SYSTEM are three completely different identifiers. System.out.println() works because System is the exact class name. Writing system.out.println() gives a compile error: 'cannot find symbol.' This applies to every identifier — class names, variable names, method names, and keywords.

items.q: Q3. Can you have multiple classes in one .java file?
items.a: Yes — a .java file can contain multiple class definitions. However, only one class can be declared public, and that public class name must match the filename. Non-public classes in the same file are accessible within the same package. In professional code, each class typically lives in its own file for maintainability.

items.q: Q4. What is the difference between a statement and an expression in Java?
items.a: An expression evaluates to a value: a + b, Math.max(5, 10), x > 0. A statement is a complete executable instruction ending with a semicolon or block: int x = 5 + 3;, System.out.println(x);. An expression becomes an expression statement when you add a semicolon: x++; Not all expressions can become statements — a + b; alone is not valid because the result is discarded with no side effect.

items.q: Q5. What is a Java record and how does it simplify syntax?
items.a: A record is a special class type introduced in Java 16 for creating immutable data carriers. Declaring record Point(int x, int y) {} automatically generates: a canonical constructor, accessor methods x() and y(), equals(), hashCode(), and toString(). What previously required 50+ lines of boilerplate now takes 1 line. Records are immutable by default — fields are final.

items.q: Q6. What are contextual keywords in Java 21?
items.a: Contextual keywords are identifiers that have special meaning only in specific syntactic contexts, but can still be used as identifiers elsewhere. Java 21 contextual keywords include: var (local variable type inference), record (data class), sealed (restricted inheritance), permits (specifies allowed subtypes), yield (switch expression value), and when (guard pattern). Unlike reserved keywords (class, int), these won't break existing code that used them as variable names.

items.q: Q7. What is the difference between // comments and /** */ Javadoc comments?
items.a: Single-line // comments are for inline code documentation — visible only in source code. Multi-line /* */ comments disable blocks or write long notes — also source-only. Javadoc /** */ comments are processed by the javadoc tool to generate professional HTML API documentation. They support @param, @return, @throws, @since, @author, and @see tags that appear in the generated documentation. All Java standard library docs (docs.oracle.com/javase) are generated this way.

items.q: Q8. Can a Java identifier start with a number?
items.a: No. Java identifiers must start with a letter (A–Z, a–z), underscore (_), or dollar sign ($). Starting with a digit like int 2name; causes a compile error. This rule exists because it prevents ambiguity — if identifiers could start with digits, the parser couldn't distinguish between the number 2 followed by identifier name, and an identifier called 2name.

items.q: Q9. Is whitespace significant in Java?
items.a: Java is not whitespace-sensitive like Python. The compiler ignores extra spaces, tabs, and blank lines between tokens. public class Hello{} and public  class  Hello {} are identical. However, whitespace is required between certain tokens — publicclass is invalid; public class is required. Indentation is a coding convention (4 spaces per level) enforced by team standards, not the compiler.

items.q: Q10. What is var in Java and is it the same as JavaScript's var?
items.a: No — Java's var (introduced in Java 10) is completely different from JavaScript's var. Java's var enables local variable type inference: the compiler determines the type from the right-hand side at compile time, and the type is fixed forever. It is still strongly and statically typed. JavaScript's var is dynamically typed and function-scoped. In Java, var x = 42 means x is permanently an int — you cannot later assign a String to it.

blocks.text: Test your understanding of Java Syntax with these practice questions. Try to answer each before revealing — active recall is the most effective way to learn.

items.q: 1. What will happen if you write int Class = 10; in Java?
items.a: This is valid! 'Class' with a capital C is not a reserved keyword — 'class' (lowercase) is. Java is case-sensitive, so 'Class' is just a regular identifier. However, this is terrible practice — naming a variable so similar to a keyword will confuse every developer who reads your code. Your IDE will likely warn you.

items.q: 2. How many public classes can exist in a single .java file?
items.a: Exactly one. A .java file can contain multiple class definitions, but only one of them may be declared public. That public class name must exactly match the filename. Other classes in the same file can have package-private (default) access. If you try to declare two public classes in one file, javac throws a compilation error.

items.q: 3. What is the output of: System.out.println("Java" + 1 + 2) and System.out.println(1 + 2 + "Java")?
items.a: First: 'Java12' — Java evaluates left-to-right. "Java" + 1 = "Java1" (String concatenation), then "Java1" + 2 = "Java12". Second: '3Java' — 1 + 2 = 3 (integer addition first), then 3 + "Java" = "3Java" (concatenation). This is a classic Java interview question testing understanding of operator evaluation order and type promotion.

items.q: 4. Rewrite this code using a Java 16+ record: class Point { int x; int y; Point(int x, int y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; } }
items.a: record Point(int x, int y) {} — This single line generates the constructor, accessors x() and y(), equals(), hashCode(), and toString() automatically. To use it: Point p = new Point(3, 4); System.out.println(p.x()); // 3 System.out.println(p); // Point[x=3, y=4]

items.q: 5. What is wrong with this identifier: int my-variable = 5;
items.a: The hyphen (-) is the subtraction operator in Java, not a valid identifier character. The compiler parses 'int my - variable = 5;' as 'int my' (incomplete declaration) minus 'variable = 5' — which produces multiple errors. Java identifiers can only contain letters, digits, underscores, and dollar signs. The correct version is: int myVariable = 5; (camelCase) or int my_variable = 5; (snake_case, uncommon in Java).

items.q: 6. Explain why var cannot be used as a method parameter type.
items.a: var was designed specifically for local variable type inference — where the compiler can definitively determine the type from the initialization expression on the right-hand side. Method parameters have no initializer at the declaration site — the type is determined only at the call site. Allowing var for parameters would require the compiler to infer types across method boundaries, which conflicts with Java's static typing model and method overloading resolution. var is also not allowed for fields, return types, or catch variables (except in catch blocks in some JEPs).

blocks.text: Java syntax is the foundation of everything you will ever write in Java. The rules you have learned in this chapter — class structure, statements, expressions, blocks, keywords, identifiers, naming conventions, and comments — apply to every single Java program from a Hello World to a Netflix-scale microservice.

The key takeaways: Java is case-sensitive, every statement ends with a semicolon, the public class name must match the filename, and keywords are reserved and cannot be reused. Follow naming conventions religiously — they are the mark of a professional Java developer.
